turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's just been a normal week, I guess. Been working a lot and trying to keep up with stuff. Nothing out of the ordinary's really been happening. Just feeling a bit... overwhelmed, I suppose.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It can be really tough to feel overwhelmed, even when things seem to be going normally on the surface. Sometimes it's the accumulation of small stressors that can add up and feel suffocating.

Can you tell me more about what you mean by "overwhelmed"? Is it feeling like you're struggling to keep up with work, or is it more of a emotional feeling, like you're feeling anxious or burnt out?

Also, when you say "trying to keep up with stuff", what kind of things are you trying to keep up with? Is it work, personal relationships, hobbies, or something else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's more of an emotional feeling, I suppose. Like, I just feel like I'm stuck in this constant state of "on" and I don't know how to turn it off. When I'm not working, I'm thinking about work, and when I'm home, I'm worrying about things that might go wrong. It's hard to explain, but it feels like everything is just piling up on me and I'm getting buried under it all.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're experiencing a sense of hypervigilance, where you're always "on" and ready to respond to potential threats or stressors, even when you're not actively working. This can be really exhausting, both mentally and emotionally.

It's like your mind is constantly racing, trying to anticipate and prepare for all the things that could go wrong, and that can make it really hard to relax and feel like you're truly "off" from work or responsibilities.

I want to acknowledge that it takes a lot of courage to admit to feeling this way, and it's great that you're recognizing that this isn't a sustainable way to live. It's okay to feel overwhelmed, and it's okay to ask for help.

One thing that might be helpful is to start exploring some strategies for managing your stress and anxiety. Have you ever tried practices like meditation, deep breathing, or journaling to help calm your mind and reduce feelings of overwhelm?

Also, I'm curious - what do you think would need to happen for you to feel like you can "turn off" and relax? Is there something specific that you think would help you feel more calm and centered?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
I've tried some of those things, but I don't know, they just don't feel like they're doing much for me. I mean, I'll try to meditate or something, but then I'll start thinking about all the things that need to be done, and I'll get anxious about not doing them right. It's hard to quiet my mind, you know?

As for what would help me feel calm, I'm not really sure. I just feel like I need to... I don't know, be more in control, I guess. It sounds stupid, but if I could just do one more thing, check one more thing, I feel like I might be able to relax. But it's hard to explain.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It can be really tough to quiet the mind, especially when you're feeling anxious or overwhelmed. It's like your brain is constantly trying to problem-solve and anticipate potential issues, and that can make it hard to relax.

I don't think it sounds stupid at all that you feel like you need to be more in control. In fact, that's a really common feeling for people who are experiencing anxiety or feelings of overwhelm. It's like your mind is trying to tell you that if you can just get everything under control, then you'll be able to relax and feel safe.

But the thing is, that's often a bit of an illusion. There's always going to be something that needs to be done, or something that could potentially go wrong. And if you're waiting for everything to be perfectly under control before you can relax, you might be waiting for a long time.

One thing that might be helpful is to start exploring the idea that you don't need to be in control all the time. That it's okay to let some things go, and to trust that everything will be okay even if you're not constantly monitoring and managing everything.

This can be a really hard concept to wrap your head around, especially if you're someone who tends to be very responsible and self-motivated. But it might be helpful to start practicing some self-compassion, and to remind yourself that it's okay to not be in control all the time.

I want to try something with you. Can you take a deep breath with me, and as you exhale, can you try to let go of just one thing that's been worrying you? Just one thing. It doesn't have to be a big thing, just something small. And as you let it go, can you try to repeat a phrase to yourself, like "I can handle whatever comes next" or "I trust that everything will be okay"?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighing) I don't know... it's hard to let go of anything when I'm feeling like this. But... okay. (pausing, taking a deep breath) I'll try. (looking down, fidgeting) I don't know why it's such a big deal, but it just is.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling gently) Ah, I think it's a great choice to start with something small like that. And it's not about the stove itself, but about the feeling of control and safety that comes with checking it. But by letting go of that one thing, you're taking a small step towards trusting that everything will be okay, even if you're not in control of every little detail. And that can be a really powerful feeling.

I want to acknowledge that it takes a lot of courage to let go of something that's been bothering you, even if it seems small. It's like you're taking a tiny risk, and that can be uncomfortable. But it's also a chance to practice self-compassion and trust that you'll be okay, even if things don't go exactly as planned.

Now, I want to ask you to take another deep breath, and as you exhale, I want you to repeat that phrase I suggested earlier: "I can handle whatever comes next." Or if that doesn't feel right for you, we can come up with a different phrase that feels more authentic. But I want you to try to say it to yourself, and see how it feels.

And remember, it's not about the stove, or the phrase, or even the feeling of control. It's about taking small steps towards trusting yourself, and learning to be kind to yourself when you're feeling overwhelmed. Can you try that for me?

It's also important to remember that you don't have to fully believe the phrase "I can handle whatever comes next" right now. It's not about convincing yourself that everything will be okay, but about taking small steps towards developing a more compassionate and trusting relationship with yourself.

By repeating that phrase, you're not trying to suppress your anxiety or pretend that everything is fine when it's not. You're actually acknowledging your fears and doubts, and gently encouraging yourself to approach them with kindness and curiosity.

It's a bit like planting a seed in the ground. You're not expecting it to grow into a full-fledged tree overnight, but you're giving it the space and nourishment it needs to grow over time. And with patience, practice, and self-compassion, you can develop a greater sense of trust and confidence in your ability to handle whatever comes your way.

I want to explore this idea further with you. What do you think would happen if you were to repeat that phrase to yourself regularly, over the next few days or weeks? Do you think it could make a difference in how you feel, or how you approach challenging situations?
